instruction.text:
You will hear an excerpt from a podcast dealing with the history of the LGBTQIA+ movement. The hosts are presenting different historic milestones, current developments and data from new surveys, several figures are mentioned.

First, read the text. Then listen to the audio file below and fill in the figures into the blanks. Name one figure each, using the exact wording used in the recording.
instruction.sound: You will hear an excerpt from a podcast dealing with the history of the LGBTQIA+ movement. The hosts are presenting different historic milestones, current developments and data from new surveys, several figures are mentioned. First, read the text. Then listen to the audio file below and fill in the figures into the blanks. Name one figure each, using the exact wording used in the recording.

atoms.a: <voice voiceLang='en' voice='m2Us_chirp'>Okay, if we move forward a bit to the present day, then we get to the big legal milestones people actually remember, right? Marriage?</voice><voice voiceLang='en' voice='f2Us_chirp'>Yep. Nationwide marriage equality is 2015—the groundbreaking Obergefell decision of the Supreme Court. And here’s where the polling layer gets interesting: Gallup’s update shows 69% of Americans say same-sex marriage should be legal.</voice><voice voiceLang='en' voice='m2Us_chirp'>So basically, “case closed,” everybody’s cool with it?</voice><voice voiceLang='en' voice='f2Us_chirp'>Not quite. The overall number hides a huge party split. In that same Gallup update, support is 83% among Democrats, and 46% among Republicans.</voice><voice voiceLang='en' voice='m2Us_chirp'>That actually explains why it can feel like the culture is constantly on fire even when a majority supports marriage equality.</voice><voice voiceLang='en' voice='f2Us_chirp'>Right—public opinion and political incentives don’t always move in sync. And also, marriage was never the finish line. Some activists worried it would become the story, and then other stuff—like workplace rights, healthcare, trans rights—gets treated like an afterthought. When you take Workplace rights for example—there is the 2020 Bostock decision. The Surpreme Court said discrimination against gay and transgender workers is covered under federal sex discrimination law. And you’d think, “Okay, that’s locked in,” but here’s the messy present-day layer: enforcement and guidance can shift even when the underlying precedent exists. </voice><voice voiceLang='en' voice='m2Us_chirp'>Is this where you’re gonna ruin my mood?</voice><voice voiceLang='en' voice='f2Us_chirp'>Just a little. In January 2026, the EEOC, that’s the US Commission for Equal Opportunities in Employment, voted to rescind its workplace harassment guidance that had spelled out protections touching LGBTQ issues—things like how harassment around gender identity gets treated. It’s not a new law, but it’s the practical “how we interpret this” handbook—and taking that away changes how protected people feel at work. The latest version of these guidelines was from 2024, so very up to date, and contained important court rulings and laws from the last 25 years. All of that has now been reversed.</voice><voice voiceLang='en' voice='m2Us_chirp'>That doesn't sound good at all.</voice><voice voiceLang='en' voice='f2Us_chirp'>Yes, unfortunately. Corporate pride has largely disappeared since Trump returned to power. But that was only ever seen as rainbow branding anyway. This divide is now much deeper. And you can see that tension in the numbers and in the backlash cycles: progress, then pushback, then progress again, then new pushback. The movement is therefore at a delicate point in its history right now.</voice>
atoms.b:
Obergefell v. Hodges was a ((2015)) landmark case that legalized same-sex marriage in the US.
((83))% say same-sex marriage should be legal, as far as Democratic voters are concerned. Among Republican voters, the figure is only ((46))%.
The EEOC guidelines that have just been repealed were last updated in ((2024)) and contained changes made over the last ((25)) years.
